## Question 1: Calibration Time for a Laboratory Instrument (4 marks)

1. The possible calibration times extend from $2$ to $8$ minutes, so the total width of the uniform distribution is
$$8-2=6\text{ minutes}$$
The uniform density forms a rectangle with total area $1$. If $h$ is its height, then
$$6h=1 \qquad \boxed{h=\frac{1}{6}}$$

2. The interval from $3.5$ to $6.2$ minutes has width
$$6.2-3.5=2.7\text{ minutes}$$
The required probability is the area of the rectangle over this interval:
$$P(3.5\leq T\leq6.2)=(\text{width})(\text{height})=(2.7)\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)=\boxed{0.450}$$

3. The two relevant intervals are disjoint. Their widths are
$$2.8-2=0.8\text{ minutes} \qquad \text{and} \qquad 8-7.4=0.6\text{ minutes}$$
Therefore
$$P(T<2.8\text{ or }T>7.4)=(0.8)\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)+(0.6)\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)=\frac{1.4}{6}\approx\boxed{0.233}$$

## Question 2: Parasitic Infection in Dogs (6 marks)

Let $I$ denote parasitic infection and let $D$ denote diarrhea.

1. The marginal and joint probabilities are
$$P(I)=\frac{90}{300}=\boxed{0.3}$$
$$P(D)=\frac{96}{300}=\boxed{0.32}$$
$$P(I\cap D)=\frac{54}{300}=\boxed{0.18}$$
2. Conditioning on diarrhea restricts the denominator to the $96$ dogs with diarrhea. Therefore
$$P(I\mid D)=\frac{P(I\cap D)}{P(D)}=\frac{0.18}{0.32}=\boxed{0.5625}$$
3. Conditioning on infection restricts the denominator to the $90$ infected dogs. Therefore
$$P(D\mid I)=\frac{P(D\cap I)}{P(I)}=\frac{0.18}{0.3}=\boxed{0.6}$$
The probabilities $P(I\mid D)$ and $P(D\mid I)$ both use the $54$ dogs in the intersection, but they use different denominators. The first conditions on the $96$ dogs with diarrhea whereas the second conditions on the $90$ dogs with an infection.


## Question 3: Recovery Time After Veterinary Anaesthesia (6 marks)

1. The recovery time is approximately Normal with
$$\mu=45\text{ minutes}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma=6\text{ minutes}$$
The standardized values of the two boundaries are
$$z_{39}=\frac{39-45}{6}=-1.00 \qquad \text{and} \qquad z_{57}=\frac{57-45}{6}=2.00$$
Therefore
$$P(39<R<57)=P(z_{39}<Z<z_{57})=P(-1.00<Z<2.00)=P(Z\leq2.00)-P(Z\leq-1.00)=N(2)-N(-1)$$
The standard Normal table gives
$$P(Z\leq-1.00)=N(-1)=1-N(1)=1-0.8413=0.1587 \qquad \text{and} \qquad P(Z\leq2.00)=0.9772$$
The probability between the two boundaries is
$$P(39<R<57)=N(2)-N(-1)=0.9772-0.1587=\boxed{0.8185}$$

2. From the standardization and table values calculated above
$$P(R<39)=P(Z<-1.00)=1-N(-1)=1-0.8413=\boxed{0.1587}$$
For the upper-tail probability
$$P(R>57)=P(Z>2.00)=1-P(Z\leq2.00)=1-N(2)=1-0.9772=\boxed{0.0228}$$

3. The expected number of recovery times between $39$ and $57$ minutes is
$$400(0.8185)=\boxed{327.4}$$
Approximately $327$ of the $400$ recovery times would be expected to fall within this interval.


## Question 4: Calibration Failures in Radiation Sensors (4 marks)

1. There are $10$ independent trials, each sensor is classified as either failing or not failing and the probability of failure is $0.08$ for every sensor. Therefore
$$X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,0.08)$$
The phrase “no more than one sensor fails” means
$$\boxed{P(X\leq1)}$$

2. The probability that no sensors fail is
$$P(X=0)=\binom{10}{0}(0.08)^0(0.92)^{10}=(0.92)^{10}\approx \boxed{0.434}$$

3. The probability that exactly one sensor fails is
$$P(X=1)=\binom{10}{1}(0.08)^1(0.92)^9=10(0.08)(0.92)^9\approx \boxed{0.378}$$

4. The events $X=0$ and $X=1$ are disjoint, so
$$P(X\leq1)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)\approx0.434388+0.377729\approx \boxed{0.812}$$
Under this model, there is approximately an $81.2\%$ probability that no more than one of the $10$ radiation sensors fails its calibration test.
